name: Concarneau
title: Concarneau Thickness Gauging for Fishing & Patrol Vessels
description: Thickness gauging in Concarneau for tuna seiners, trawlers, patrol vessels and yard-repair ships: hull plating, tanks and piping measured by UTM at the quay.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Ships at Concarneau
intro: Concarneau is a small port with a large shipbuilding and repair tradition, known for its tuna fleet, its fishing boats and the shipyard that builds and refits patrol vessels and working craft. Ships that come here for repair or a landing are held in one place long enough to be measured. Atlantis mobilises technicians from India to the quay, planning the work around yard schedules and the tide.

highlights.p: Concarneau has long been a base for tuna fishing and coastal trawling. Large steel hulls on long voyages need their plating, tanks and piping measured when they come back to the quay.

highlights.h: A shipyard that builds and repairs
highlights.p: Vessels in the yard's hands, from patrol craft to workboats, can be measured early in the stay. A steel list drawn up on day one keeps the repair specification honest.

highlights.h: Measured steel for owners deciding on renewal
highlights.p: Many hulls here are mid-life or older. Readings give owners a basis for choosing between a steel renewal programme, a planned refit and replacing the vessel.

port.h: Concarneau: fishing port and shipyard town
p: Concarneau lies on the southern coast of Finistère, in a sheltered bay on the Breton coast, with an old walled island town, the Ville Close, at the entrance to its harbour. The port is a working one: a fishing harbour with a fish market, a commercial quay for small cargo and a shipyard whose cranes and sheds dominate part of the waterfront. The harbour is tidal, with moderate tidal range by Channel standards, and its approaches are marked and pilotage-friendly for small and mid-sized vessels. It is not a port for large deep-sea cargo ships.

Two fleets define the traffic. The first is the fishing fleet: coastal boats, trawlers, and the large tuna seiners that fish far from home and return for refit and crew change. These are big steel vessels, and they spend weeks at sea in warm water, which is hard on tanks, hull plating and piping. The second is the group of ships that come to the shipyard, which builds, converts and repairs patrol vessels, offshore support craft, tugs and fishing vessels, and also works for owners from overseas. Small passenger boats serve the nearby islands in summer.

For inspection, the port offers the benefit of dwell time and concentrated services. A tuna seiner back from a long voyage stays at the quay for a period of refit and restocking, and the repair yard has the staging, power and lighting to support access to hull and tanks. A patrol vessel being refitted can be measured at the yard's berth. Ships needing a major dry docking may go to a larger yard in Brest, Lorient or Saint-Nazaire, and readings taken at Concarneau help them to prepare. The quiet bay and the sheltered quays mean weather rarely stops the work on shore.

facilities.h: Where gauging can be done at Concarneau
p: The shipyard's berths and repair quays are the main place for thickness work. A vessel in for repair afloat has its tanks emptied and ventilated by the yard as part of the programme, and hull plating below the waterline can be measured on the sections exposed by the yard's lifting and dock arrangements. The superintendent and the yard agree the sequence, and the technicians measure compartments as they are released so renewal decisions are taken early. Steel found below the owner's allowable diminution is marked in the plan before the cutting begins.

At the fishing quays a seiner or trawler lies alongside between voyages, and its decks, fish holds, fuel and ballast tanks and accessible piping can be gauged. The commercial quay offers the same for small coasters. Because the harbour is small, access to a vessel is usually a matter of a gangway rather than a launch. For ships waiting outside the harbour for a berth or a tide, a launch can be arranged by the agent or the harbour authority. The sea state in the bay is mostly manageable, though Atlantic swell can arrive in winter.
list: Shipyard berths and repair quays — hull, tank and piping gauging on patrol vessels, tugs, workboats and fishing vessels in repair.
Fishing quays — tuna seiner and trawler plating, fish hold, fuel tank and piping readings between voyages.
Commercial quay — hold, coaming and hatch cover gauging on small coasters during discharge or loading.
Harbour anchorage and outer berths — launch-served readings on vessels waiting for a quay space or the tide.
Island ferry berths — deck and tank checks on small passenger craft during the off-season.

context.h: Regulation and the fishing and patrol fleets
p: France applies Paris MoU port state control, and the Centres de sécurité des navires of the French maritime administration oversee safety on French-flag fishing vessels and coastal craft. A tuna seiner returning from months at sea faces a thorough check of its hull and systems, and an owner who has measured the plating in advance can plan repair work on his own timetable. Foreign-flag ships calling in the harbour follow the same risk-based targeting as at any Paris MoU port.

Patrol vessels and naval-style craft built in Concarneau are delivered to government customers under their own acceptance and class arrangements, and the shipyard's quality control and the customer's inspectors remain the route for that work. For owners of fishing vessels, thickness readings support voluntary classification and the decision to renew steel. EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime affect larger ships on EU voyages, and the EU Ship Recycling Regulation's Inventory of Hazardous Materials applies to ships calling at EU ports. Older hulls on long voyages are the ones where measured steel is most valuable.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Concarneau
jobs.p: Most Concarneau jobs are connected to a yard stay or a period alongside between voyages. The owner or superintendent tells us what the vessel does, the age of the hull, the class or flag requirements and any known problem areas, and we plan the readings around what the yard releases and when. Typical requests include:
list: Hull plating, fish hold and ballast tank gauging on a tuna seiner back from a long voyage, ahead of its refit.
Early steel assessment on a vessel entering the shipyard for repair, so the work list reflects the measured wastage.
Fuel tank and bilge piping wall-thickness checks on a trawler during a quay stay, with gauging of the engine room structure.
Hull and deck gauging on a patrol vessel or workboat during a yard refit, supporting the owner's own record.
Condition gauging for a prospective buyer of a second-hand fishing vessel or coastal ship lying at the quay.

logistics: Quimper-Cornouaille airport, near Concarneau, has connections to Paris, and from India the practical route is a flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle followed by a domestic flight or a train towards Quimper and a road transfer to the port. The shipyard or the ship's agent arranges access to the quays and the repair berths. France is in the Schengen area, so every technician needs a Schengen visa, which we apply for once the yard stay or the landing period is firm, together with an invitation letter from the owner or yard naming the vessel.
vessels: Patrol vessels and offshore support craft

faqs.q: Can a tuna seiner be gauged when it returns to Concarneau?
faqs.a: Yes. A seiner stays at the quay for refit and restocking, and its hull plating, fish holds, fuel and ballast tanks and piping can be measured during that period. The crew or the yard ventilate and prepare the tanks, and we measure them as they are released so the owner can decide on repairs early.

faqs.q: Do you work on vessels inside the shipyard?
faqs.a: We work for the owner or manager of a vessel that is in the yard, not as a subcontractor to the yard. Access, staging and lighting are arranged with the yard, and readings are reported by compartment so that the repair specification is based on measured steel.

faqs.q: Is a major drydocking possible at Concarneau?
faqs.a: The yard handles repair and refit of small and mid-sized vessels. Larger ships needing a major docking usually go to Brest, Lorient or Saint-Nazaire. Gauging at Concarneau beforehand gives that yard a measured steel list and helps to shorten the stay in dock.

faqs.q: What other checks can be done with hull gauging on a fishing vessel?
faqs.a: Magnetic particle or dye penetrant testing on winch foundations, gantry and net-drum supports is common, as is ultrasonic testing of weld repairs. Wall-thickness checks on fuel, bilge and sea-water piping fit the same visit, because the access and permits are already in place.
